title: Adaptive TTL slope and refresh matrix
content:
Purpose:
This is a personal sketch for an adaptive TTL (time-to-live) / refresh matrix feature for Redwood's serving runtime. Aim: reduce stale output risk for high-value requests while minimizing refresh/cold model invocations and keeping tail latency predictable.

Quick problem statement:
- Some requests (high-cost or high-provenance prompts) need fresher model outputs than typical cached responses.
- Static TTLs are too coarse: either blow up model calls or keep stale content.
- Need a gearshiftable policy that can be expressed per-route/tenant, runtime-configured, and backed by telemetry.

Design goals:
- Expressiveness: per-route or per-tenant TTL + slope + refresh budget.
- Operational safety: soft-fallbacks, circuit-breakers for refresh storms.
- Observability: metrics for refresh rate, hit/miss, staleness incidents, SLO impact.
- Simple rollout: feature flags + canary policy with traffic percentage.

Terminology (working):
- TTL base: minimum guaranteed cache TTL for a key.
- TTL slope: an increasing function that lengthens TTL for keys with repeated hits (hotness).
- Freshness threshold: application-level acceptable staleness score.
- Refresh: a background revalidation call that updates cached entry before TTL expiry.
- On-demand requery: immediate model call when staleness exceeds threshold and user triggers explicit refresh.

High-level architecture (ascii):

 client --> router --> local-cache layer (TTL slope) --> serving runtime --> model
                   |                               ^
                   |----> refresh scheduler ------> |\

Refresh scheduler: keeps short-term queue of entries nearing expiration and triggers background model calls respecting concurrency and refresh budget.

Policy surface (API sketch) - TTLPolicy v0 (JSON shape planned):

{
  "policy_id": "string",
  "scope": "route|tenant|global",
  "ttl_base_seconds": 30,            // base TTL in seconds
  "ttl_slope": {                      // controls growth with repeated hits
    "type": "linear|log|step",
    "params": "..."                 // string-encoded for runtime parsing for now
  },
  "refresh": {
    "enabled": true,
    "budget_per_minute": 5,           // global or per-route budget
    "concurrency_limit": 2,
    "strategy": "proactive|reactive|hybrid"
  },
  "staleness_threshold": 0.35,        // unitless heuristic (0..1)
  "fallback": {
    "allow_stale_on_error": true,
    "max_stale_seconds": 300
  }
}

Notes on fields:
- ttl_slope.type=linear => TTL = ttl_base + k * hit_count (cap applied)
- step => TTL jumps after hit_count crosses thresholds. Useful for session-based contexts.
- params can be a short CSV for now, later promote to typed object.

State machine for an entry (text table):
- COLD (miss) -> SERVE + CACHE (TTL=ttl_base) -> HOT (repeat hits) -> SLOPE_APPLY -> LONG_TTL
- If staleness_score > staleness_threshold && refresh.strategy != proactive => schedule on-demand refresh or mark for immediate requery (depending on request weight).

Refresh strategies (notes):
- proactive: refresh scheduler picks hot keys within budget; good for predictable hot traffic (chat threads).
- reactive: when a request notices staleness > threshold, it triggers a refresh (may add some tail latency).
- hybrid: proactive for hot keys, reactive fallback for sudden spikes.

Telemetry & metrics to emit (minimal):
- ttl.policy_applied{policy_id,scope}
- cache.hit, cache.miss
- refresh.scheduled, refresh.completed, refresh.failed
- refresh.latency_p50/90/99
- staleness.incident_count (when served content > threshold)
- model_calls_from_refresh vs model_calls_from_ingress (to track cost shifting)

Operational safety knobs:
- global_refresh_budget: hard cap enforced cluster-wide to avoid stampedes during large invalidation.
- refresh_backoff: exponential backoff per-key after N failures.
- canary_percent: allow policy to apply to X% of traffic initially.
- kill-switch: immediate disable for policy_id.

Example YAML-like config snippets (for console or private deployments):

policy:
  id: "customer-chat-ttl-v1"
  scope: "tenant:acme"
  ttl_base_seconds: 20
  ttl_slope:
    type: "log"
    params: "k=6,cap=3600"
  refresh:
    enabled: true
    budget_per_minute: 12
    concurrency_limit: 3
    strategy: "hybrid"
  staleness_threshold: 0.2
  fallback:
    allow_stale_on_error: false
    max_stale_seconds: 120

Runtime enforcement pseudocode (very rough):

on_request(key):
  meta = cache.get_meta(key)
  if !meta: return MISS
  hit_count = meta.hits_since_write
  ttl = compute_ttl(ttl_base, slope, hit_count)
  if now - meta.last_write > ttl:
    staleness = compute_staleness_score(meta)
    if staleness > policy.staleness_threshold:
      if policy.refresh.strategy == "proactive":
        refresh_scheduler.enqueue(key)
        return meta.value if fallback.allow_stale_on_error else MISS
      else:
        // reactive or on-demand
        if within_budget():
          val = requery_model(key)
          cache.write(key,val)
          return val
        else:
          return meta.value

Open questions / tradeoffs (brain dump):
- How to compute staleness_score? Options: age-based heuristic, semantic drift estimate (cheap embedding comparison), or external signal (user feedback). Age-only is simplest.
- Accounting for per-token cost of refreshes: should we weight budget by estimated token cost? Probably yes for large gen calls.
- Session-scoped keys: TTL slope should probably be reset on session end. Need lifecycle hook.
- Privacy: caching of prompt+response may need redaction for regulated tenants. Policy scope must support privacy flags.

Rollout plan (quick):
1) Implement policy shape + minimal enforcement in local cache layer behind feature flag.
2) Add telemetry and burn-in on internal low-traffic routes.
3) Canary mixing: policy applies to 1% -> 10% -> 50% with guardrails watching refresh model_call ratio.
4) Opt-in console UI to craft policy for tenant/route.

Short-term experiments I want to run (notes):
- Simulated workload where 5% of keys are cold, 10% hot; measure model_call rate delta when slope enabled vs static TTL.
- Semantic staleness: compute embedding distance between cached output and freshly requery; see correlation with age heuristic.
- Cost-aware budget: experiment with weighting refresh budget by estimated output length.

Scratch TODOs (personal):
- [ ] Pick canonical staleness formula and add to proto
- [ ] Implement lightweight refresh scheduler with Redis priority queue prototype
- [ ] Add tests for concurrency_limit enforcement
- [ ] Draft console UI mock for policy composer (small form)
- [ ] Wire canary flags and kill-switch into rollout pipeline

Notes-to-self: keep this in users/ — probably split into two follow-ups: one doc for "policy/api" and another for "scheduler implementation". Later convert to product PRD if sparks fly.

References/links I've been eyeballing:
- Slack thread: #runtime-refresh-design (link in linked_artifacts)
- Prior ticket: JIRA-INFRA-789 (linked above)
- Prototype PR: github.com/redwood-inference/routing/pull/456

End of sketch.
